content.content:
## 1. The specification

### 1.1 `widen` itself: not named

- No chapter of `Specification/` names `ZZ`'s `widen`. `grep -rnw widen Specification/` finds two other things only. One is a user function `widen[\T, S extends T\](c: C[\S\]): C[\T\]`, the revival's example for the exclusion rule (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:433-443`, commit `3924e7ec3`). The other is the revival's Appendix I entry on the natives, which lists `ZZ32`'s `widen` among the 21 bindings moved onto helpers (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:4467-4472`). `ZZ32`'s `widen` is exact, so it raises the question nowhere.
- The Working Draft of February 2011 names no `widen` (`grep -rnw widen Specification-1.0-frozen/`: nothing). Its integer chapter has no fixed-size integer type at all: it lists `ZZ`, `ZZ*` and their refinements by sign (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:16-68`).
- The team's later restart has no `widen` either (`grep -rnw widen Documentation/`: nothing).
- Row 349's citation column and row 502's history give the same finding: "no prose chapter names `widen`" (`explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`, row 502).

### 1.2 Overflow: the general sentence and how far it reaches

The sentence, as the revised text has it:

    The handling of overflow depends on the type of the number produced.
    For integer results, overflow throws an \TYP{IntegerOverflow}.
    Rational computations do not overflow.

- Where it stands. It appears twice, in the subsections "Multiplication, Division, Modulo, and Remainder Operators" (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:113`, sentence at `:154-155`) and "Addition and Subtraction Operators" (`:190`, sentence at `:195-196`). Both are about operators. The Working Draft has it word for word at the same lines (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:154-155`, `:195-196`). So does the team's later restart (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/Operators/operator-overview.tick:154-155`, `:195-196`).
- Wrapping has its own spelling. Each of the two subsections then says: "Wraparound addition and subtraction on fixed-size integers are expressed by ∔ and ∸. Saturating addition and subtraction ... by ⊞ and ⊟. These operations do not overflow." (`opr-overview.tex:205-209`; for multiplication, ⨰, and ⊡ or ⊠, `:172-176`). Both texts have these sentences.
- How far the revival has read it. The revised text applies "the rule for integer results above" to `GCD` and `LCM` (`opr-overview.tex:262-270`, callout `revival-gcd`). It also applies it to a `ZZ` shift too large to represent (`Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:738-739`) and to an integer power that is no integer (`:537`). P-73 reads it under walk as covering "every operation whose result can leave its type" (section 5).
- No passage applies it to a conversion, or exempts conversions from it.

### 1.3 Conversions between integer types, and `narrow`

The revised integer chapter, lines the revival wrote:

    An integer type coerces from each other integer type all of whose values it holds,
    as listed above; every other conversion between integer types is written explicitly.

    Among the explicit conversions, the method \VAR{narrow} converts a value of
    \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and a value of
    \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} to \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, by keeping its low 32 bits ...
    A value that the narrower type holds is unchanged; any other wraps, and no
    \TYP{IntegerOverflow} is thrown.

(`Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:36-37`, `:39-45`.)

- The callout `revival-shifts` says: "The Working Draft of February 2011 named neither `narrow` nor `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT`, ... the two paragraphs above state the rules the revival decided for them" (`basic-integers.tex:63-66`).
- The Appendix I entry "Shifts and narrowing on the integer types" (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:1723` onward) gives the reason. `narrow` "keeps the low 32 bits as the team's own test asserts at the values 2^64-1 and 2^63 (`ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss`, lines 210-211), on the signed types as on the unsigned" (`changes.tex:1760-1762`).
- So `ZZ`'s `narrow`, the sibling of `widen` in the same trait, is stated to wrap. `ZZ`'s `widen` is the one explicit conversion out of `ZZ` that the text leaves unstated. The rung that wrote the paragraph left it out on purpose: "`ZZ`'s `widen`, which walk also truncates to 64 bits (`BigNum.java:292-296`), is not stated: no decision covers it and its name promises no truncation; it is reported here and not chosen" (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-integer-rules/decision-record.md:42`).
- The coercion chapter's revision callout gives the revival's rule for the number types: "a conversion between number types is a coercion where it is exact and stays explicit where it can lose precision" (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:74-80`). It says which conversions are written out. It does not say what a written-out conversion does with a value that does not fit.

### 1.4 A conversion that the specification declares as throwing

- The binary-words chapter declares a conversion from a word to an integer with a `throws` clause: `signedIndex(): IndexInt throws { IntegerOverflow }` and `unsignedIndex(): IndexInt throws { IntegerOverflow }`. They are in `trait BasicBinaryOperations`, at `Specification/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1230-1231`, `:1292-1293` and `:1478-1479`. The Working Draft has them at the same lines.
- Their description is "[Description to be supplied.]", and the library does not build them.
- They are the specification's only conversion into an integer type that says what happens when the value does not fit, and what they say is `IntegerOverflow`.

### 1.5 Where the Working Draft differs

- The Working Draft has no fixed-size integer types in its integer chapter, and no `narrow`, `widen`, coercion between integer types or shift rule. All of section 1.3 is the revival's text.
- The general sentence (1.2) and the binary-words declarations (1.4) are the same in both texts.
- `IntegerOverflow` appears in the Working Draft only at the general sentence, the binary words and one method entry (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:777`).

Each line was measured here, except where marked. Java is OpenJDK 25.0.4.1; Scala is the tree's `scala-library-2.13.18.jar`; Rust is rustc 1.97.0; Python is 3.13.16 with NumPy 2.5.3.

- **Java**: `BigInteger.longValue()` keeps the low 64 bits; `longValueExact()` throws `ArithmeticException`. The cast `(int) aLong` truncates; `Math.toIntExact` throws.
- **Scala**: `BigInt.toLong` keeps the low 64 bits. Scala has no checked conversion, only the test `isValidLong`.
- **Swift** (not run; read in `swiftlang/swift`, `stdlib/public/core/Integers.swift` on `main`, fetched 2026-10-31):
  - The plain conversion `Int64(x)` from any `BinaryInteger` traps: "If the value passed as `source` is not representable in this type, a runtime error may occur" (`:582-583`), and "Not enough bits to represent the passed value" (`:3427`).
  - The low bits are spelled `Int64(truncatingIfNeeded:)` (`:633`), saturation `Int64(clamping:)` (`:3136`), and the test `Int64(exactly:)`, which gives `nil`.
- **Rust**:
  - Primitives: `x as i64` from an `i128` keeps the low 64 bits; `i64::try_from` gives `Err(TryFromIntError(PosOverflow))`.
  - The standard library has no bignum. The `num-bigint` crate's `BigInt::to_i64` returns `Option<i64>`, `None` out of range, and its `TryFrom<&BigInt>` fails. It offers no truncating conversion (read in `rust-num/num-bigint`, `src/bigint/convert.rs:41-55`, `:107-132`, fetched 2026-10-31; not run).
- **Python**: `int` is unbounded and has no 64-bit type. At the places it narrows, `ctypes.c_int64(2**64+5).value` keeps the low bits (5). `struct.pack('<q', ...)`, `int.to_bytes(8, ..., signed=True)` and `numpy.int64(...)` raise (`struct.error`, `OverflowError`).
- **Julia**, which P-66 names (not run; by its documentation): `Int64(big(2)^64)` throws `InexactError`, and the low bits are spelled `x % Int64`. X10, which P-66 also names, was not checked.

In short: Java's `longValue` and Scala's `toLong`, the plain methods of their bignums, keep the low bits, and Java also offers the checked `longValueExact`. Rust's `as` between primitive integers keeps the low bits too. Of the languages that P-66 names, Swift (read in its source) and Julia (by its documentation) make the plain conversion checked and spell the low bits separately, and Rust's bignum crate (read in its source) offers only checked conversions. Python has no 64-bit integer of its own, and its narrowing places split: `ctypes` keeps the low bits, `struct`, `to_bytes` and NumPy raise.

content.content:
**The decision, and it is a decision: `narrow` throws `IntegerOverflow` when the value does not fit, on both the signed and the unsigned side.** Four things argue for it. The file's own convention, counted above: thirty-two plainly-named members of the four numeric traits take an Overflowing native, and the wrapping and saturating spellings take the other two. This world's own signed narrowing, `asZZ32` at `:576`, already throws, so a truncating `narrow` would put two plainly-named signed narrowings with different answers in one trait. The team's own import block reserved all three unsigned narrowings and used none, so the plain slot was left open and the convention says which of the three fills it. And the specification's twice-stated rule that an integer result that does not fit throws `IntegerOverflow`, with truncation given its own spelling elsewhere.

**What the alternative costs, since the alternative has real evidence behind it.** Truncating on the unsigned side is what the interpreter does (`UnsignedLong.java:230-234`) and what `ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss:210-211` assert, at the deliberately chosen out-of-range values 2^63 and 2^64-1: `widen(narrow(-x1)) = (x1 LSHIFT 32)-1` and `widen(narrow(x1 LSHIFT 63)) = x0`. Those two lines are gated: `ProjectFortress/tests/` holds 383 `.fss` and no `.test` file at all, and `FileTests.interpreterSuite("tests", true, false)` (`FileTests.java:768`) runs every one of them directly, so an `assert` that fails there turns `ant testSystem` red. The file passes today — measured, `probes/walk-unsignedtest.txt`, `PASS?` and exit 0. So choosing to throw makes those two assertions a walk-against-compiled divergence on the day `UnsignedTest.fss` compiles, and the specification does not settle it because it does not mention `narrow`. That divergence is measured both ways here and carried as provisional ledger row W-2; it is the price of the decision and it is not hidden. The two remaining arguments for truncating are weaker than they look: the interpreter's signed narrow raises an uncatchable Java-level error rather than a Fortress exception (measured, `probes/walk-narrow.txt`), so the glue is not a careful witness on this point; and the asymmetry it would install has no statement anywhere in the tree to support it.

## The failing test, and the pass
**D3, deferred, home 3 — under `walk`, a signed `narrow` that overflows cannot be caught.** Measured both ways, `probes/probe-NarrowSigned.txt` and `probes/walk-narrow.txt`: the interpreter's `Int.rc` raises `error("Overflow of ZZ32 " + i)` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java:239-245`), which arrives as a `com.sun.fortress.exceptions.ProgramError` and is **not** caught by `try … catch e IntegerOverflow ⇒ …`, so a program that guards the conversion dies anyway; on the compiled path the same guard prints `true`. Here the specification does settle it, and against the interpreter: `Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:155` says an integer overflow throws an `IntegerOverflow`; `basic/exceptions.tex:73-74` says every exception is a subtype of `CheckedException` or `UncheckedException`, and `CompilerBuiltin.fsi:749` makes `IntegerOverflow` an `UncheckedException`; and `basic/expressions/try.tex:56-60` says a thrown exception "is matched against the subclauses of the `catch` clause in turn, exactly as in a `typecase` expression". A thrown `IntegerOverflow` is therefore catchable by a `catch e IntegerOverflow` clause, and under `walk` it is not. The repair is `Int.rc` raising a Fortress exception instead of calling `error`, which is Java and outside a library rung — rule 4's fourth case, so the rung lands and opens provisional ledger row **W-3**.

An integer type coerces from each other integer type all of whose values it holds,
as listed above; every other conversion between integer types is written explicitly.

Among the explicit conversions, the method \VAR{narrow} converts a value of
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and a value of
\EXP{\mathbb{N}64} to \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, by keeping its low 32 bits: the result
is the value of the narrower type that is congruent to the argument modulo
\EXP{2^{32}}.
A value that the narrower type holds is unchanged; any other wraps, and no
\TYP{IntegerOverflow} is thrown.

content.content: - P-66 **The integer principle: Java's and the JVM's defaults stay where they make sense, and are corrected where they fail high performance or mathematical precision.** The team did so with rounding. A hardware behaviour that bytecode can express gets its own explicit spelling, as the specification's wrapping and saturating operators do. Where the JVM prevents a correct implementation, the project gives way for now. The peers to compare are Julia, X10, Swift and Rust.

### What you were told

- 2026-09-19, 17:29. The question came as item 7 of seven: "what `narrow` does out of range". The default: "the rung decides and records it, you see it at landing." - Rung W's worker chose to raise `IntegerOverflow`. It opened ledger row 346.
- 2026-09-22, 05:03. Row 43 of the fourteen rows. You were told: the compiled path throws; the interpreter truncates; the team's test expects truncation. The advice: "truncate on both, one prelude body; the team's unused helper says they meant wrapping." You said that you must review all the rows in detail (05:21).
- 2026-09-22, 06:02. Row 43 in one paragraph. The same advice. You asked to go row by row, with refreshers and with what other languages do (06:16).
- 2026-09-22, 21:35. Row 43 in the nine moves. This is the text that you approved.
  - The question: keep the low 32 bits, or refuse.
  - The case: `NN64` to `NN32`. "the signed sibling has the same question and should get the same answer."
  - The two paths: "The interpreter keeps the low bits: a plain cast." The compiled path throws, by rung W's choice.
  - The specification: "Nothing. The word `narrow` appears in no chapter." Only the general rule: an ordinary integer result throws on overflow.
  - Where `narrow` is declared: on `NN64`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ` and `RR64`.
  - The library never narrows a value out of range.
  - The team's test: two lines by Steele, 2008-07-21, chosen to test truncation.
  - The peers: Java, Kotlin and C truncate. Swift and Julia refuse, and spell truncation explicitly. Rust's `as` truncates; its checked conversion gives an error. "Split, with the modern trend toward refusing by default."
  - The derivation: your principle, put as "mathematical meaning for arithmetic and hardware meaning, explicitly spelled, for bit operations". On the unsigned types, keeping the low bits was called a bit operation. Swift's shape "would mean editing Steele's test".
  - The advice: "truncate on both paths, one prelude body, with the signed sibling checked to match. Rung W's choice on this point is reversed."
- 2026-09-22, 21:36. You asked "Rung W?". You were told: its worker chose the throw under a silent specification; the choice "was the worker's [...] and never yours"; reversing it "costs one line". You got the path of rung W's record.
- 2026-09-23, 07:42 and 23:58. Rider 2. You were told: "Read plainly", your decision makes the signed `narrow`, `ZZ64` to `ZZ32`, truncate too. That "reverses one more prelude body and three of rung W's assertions". The advice: no to the rider.

### What you decided, in your own words

- 2026-09-22, sent 21:48:12, delivered 21:49:15: "Row 43 approved as recommended."
- 2026-09-24, 00:06: "With the above recommendations you proposed (go, yes, no), launch Batch 3.5 workflow". The "no" declined rider 2. So the signed `narrow` truncates too.
- You gave no reason of your own in these two messages. The reasons in the advice were the coordinator's.
- The derivation applied your words of that morning, on the shifts:
  - 07:17: "we should use Java or JVM defaults where it makes sense, but We shouldn't be shy to correct the mistakes of, of JVM when seen through the lens of high performance and mathematical precision uh, language."
  - 07:17: "if there are gaps in a library where it is possible to express something that is done in hardware, like the trapping operators the Swift is using, if, if it's possible to express those on, on JVM in bytecode, we should do that."
  - 07:31: "if every other language does something else, that's uh, the clearest red flag to stop and pause and reconsider."

### What you were not told, that bears on the question today

1. `ZZ`'s own `narrow` and `widen`.
   - The 21:35 text named `ZZ` once, in the list of types that declare `narrow`. It did not say what `ZZ`'s `narrow` does. It did not name `ZZ`'s `widen`.
   - It said: "Widening always fits." That is false for `ZZ`'s `widen`. It goes from `ZZ` to `ZZ64` and can lose bits (row 502).
   - P-72 covers `ZZ64` to `ZZ32` and `NN64` to `NN32` only.
   - On 2026-09-28 the specification rung wrote that `ZZ`'s `narrow` keeps the low 32 bits too. It read P-72 as a general rule. You did not decide the `ZZ` case.
2. Who wrote them, and when.
   - Crink wrote `ZZ`'s `narrow` and `widen` on 2009-09-10 (`e1567d62f`). He reverted them the same day (`02e648434`) and put them back on 2009-09-11 (`8d2eb48f5`).
   - His commit message: "The nomenclature needs work, in my opinion. Incidentally, my first ever use of Java."
   - His comment on `widen`: "This routine, named for consistency, converts to a ZZ64".
   - `research/authorship.md:68` leaves Crink unresolved: "likely external SCA contributor".
   - You were told only who wrote the test: Steele.
3. The team's own signed `narrow` refused.
   - You were told: "The interpreter keeps the low bits: a plain cast." That was true for `NN64` only.
   - The team's walk `ZZ64` `narrow` called `Int.rc`. It stopped the run with "Overflow of ZZ32". This code is in the team's tree from 2008-03-24 (`1d2680d4d`) or earlier to its last commit, `a874948ac`.
   - Rung W's record said so (`rung-int-conversions/record.md:25`, row 347). The 21:35 text and rider 2 did not.
   - P-72's signed half removed that check on 2026-09-24 (`d6faad28f`).
4. Steele's checked `asZZ32` of 2011.
   - On 2011-09-08 Steele changed the compiled prelude's `asZZ32` from `jLongToInt` to `jLongOverflowingToInt` (`9ce7d8189`). The same commit made `+`, `-`, `·`, `DIV`, negation and absolute value on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` checked.
   - Rung W's `narrow` copied that body. Rung W gave four reasons for the throw (`rung-int-conversions/REPORT.md:74`). In the prelude, a plainly named operation checks. `asZZ32` checks. The team bound the unsigned helpers and used none. The specification has its general rule.
   - The 21:35 text gave the last reason only. It did not name `asZZ32`.
   - Today the compiled `trait ZZ64` has two conversions to `ZZ32` with two answers: `asZZ32` throws, `narrow` keeps the low bits (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:581`, `:659`; F-124).
5. The specification is silent on conversions, not only on `narrow`.
   - You were told that the word `narrow` is in no chapter. That is correct.
   - You were not told: no passage says what any written-out conversion does with a value that does not fit. The Working Draft's integer chapter has no fixed-size types.
   - One exception: the binary-words chapter declares `signedIndex()` and `unsignedIndex()` with `throws { IntegerOverflow }` (`Specification/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1292-1293`, `:1478-1479`). It describes neither, and the library does not build them.
6. The peers.
   - You were told the peers for the fixed-size types. That summary was fair.
   - You were not told the peers for an unbounded integer, the `ZZ` case. Java: `BigInteger.longValue()` keeps the low bits, `longValueExact()` throws. Scala: `BigInt.toLong` keeps the low bits. Swift: the plain conversion traps; the low bits are `truncatingIfNeeded:`. Julia: the plain conversion throws `InexactError`; the low bits are `x % Int64`. Rust: the `num-bigint` crate gives only checked conversions. (`explorations/reviews/widen-evidence.md`, section 7.)
   - Of the four peers that your principle names (P-66: Julia, X10, Swift, Rust), Swift and Julia check the plain conversion. Nobody checked X10.

### My judgements

These are mine, not the record's and not yours.

- The 21:35 text said: "Rung W's own unused import of the wrapping helper says the same." Rung W's report reads the same import block the other way: seven natives bound, one used, and that one checks (`REPORT.md:52`). I see no evidence of intent in an unused import.

Read so, keeping the low bits is a hardware behaviour. That points to Swift's shape: a checked plain conversion, and a low-bits conversion with its own name. Your own words at 07:17 name Swift's trapping operators.

The team's walk arithmetic on the fixed-size types wrapped (2026-09-23 07:42 text: "the interpreter's silently wrapping `+`, `-`, `·`"). So the 2008 test shows `narrow` in a world that wrapped. In 2011 Steele made the compiled prelude's arithmetic and `asZZ32` checked.
- At 06:49 on 2026-09-23 you were told: "No crossing on row 43". The queue line shows that you sent your approval at 21:48:12, before the coordinator's 21:48:38 "Row 43 still waits on your word". The gap that you felt was real. It does not change what you had read before you approved: the texts of 21:35:51 and 21:36:35.

- Rung W (climb batch 2, 2026-09-20) added `widen`, `narrow`, `unsigned` and `signed` to the compiler's prelude, on the four fixed-size types, because ladder files needed them (the 21:36:35 text). Its worker chose the throw and opened row 346. The re-approval table brought it to you as row 43.

## Part 2, word for word

### What you were told

- 2026-09-19, 17:29. The question came as item 7 of seven: "what `narrow` does out of range". The default: "the rung decides and records it, you see it at landing." You said that you could not decide in that form. At 17:53 the coordinator wrote: "Everything else is mine." The question left your table.
- 2026-09-20, 05:28. You asked for batch 2's goals. You were told that the rung "has to decide what `narrow` does out of range, since the specification is silent." You said "Go".
- Rung W's worker chose to raise `IntegerOverflow`. It opened ledger row 346.
- 2026-09-22, 05:03. Row 43 of the fourteen rows. You were told: the compiled path throws; the interpreter truncates; the team's test expects truncation. The advice: "truncate on both, one prelude body; the team's unused helper says they meant wrapping." You said that you must review all the rows in detail (05:21).
- 2026-09-22, 06:02. Row 43 in one paragraph. The same advice. You asked to go row by row, with refreshers and with what other languages do (06:16).
- 2026-09-22, 21:35. Row 43 in the nine moves. This is the text that you approved.
  - The question: keep the low 32 bits, or refuse.
  - The case: `NN64` to `NN32`. "the signed sibling has the same question and should get the same answer."
  - The two paths: "The interpreter keeps the low bits: a plain cast." The compiled path throws, by rung W's choice.
  - The specification: "Nothing. The word `narrow` appears in no chapter." Only the general rule: an ordinary integer result throws on overflow.
  - Where `narrow` is declared: on `NN64`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ` and `RR64`.
  - The library never narrows a value out of range.
  - The team's test: two lines by Steele, 2008-07-21, chosen to test truncation.
  - The peers: Java, Kotlin and C truncate. Swift and Julia refuse, and spell truncation explicitly. Rust's `as` truncates; its checked conversion gives an error. "Split, with the modern trend toward refusing by default."
  - The derivation: your principle, put as "mathematical meaning for arithmetic and hardware meaning, explicitly spelled, for bit operations". On the unsigned types, keeping the low bits was called a bit operation. Swift's shape "would mean editing Steele's test".
  - The advice: "truncate on both paths, one prelude body, with the signed sibling checked to match. Rung W's choice on this point is reversed."
- 2026-09-22, 21:36. You asked "Rung W?". You were told: its worker chose the throw under a silent specification; the choice "was the worker's [...] and never yours"; reversing it "costs one line". You got the path of rung W's record.
- 2026-09-23, 07:42 and 23:58. Rider 2. You were told: "Read plainly", your decision makes the signed `narrow`, `ZZ64` to `ZZ32`, truncate too. That "reverses one more prelude body and three of rung W's assertions". The advice: no to the rider.

### What you decided, in your own words

- 2026-09-22, sent 21:48:12, delivered 21:49:15: "Row 43 approved as recommended."
- 2026-09-24, 00:06: "With the above recommendations you proposed (go, yes, no), launch Batch 3.5 workflow". The "no" declined rider 2. So the signed `narrow` truncates too.
- You gave no reason of your own in these two messages. The reasons in the advice were the coordinator's.
- The derivation applied your words of that morning, on the shifts:
  - 07:17: "we should use Java or JVM defaults where it makes sense, but We shouldn't be shy to correct the mistakes of, of JVM when seen through the lens of high performance and mathematical precision uh, language."
  - 07:17: "if there are gaps in a library where it is possible to express something that is done in hardware, like the trapping operators the Swift is using, if, if it's possible to express those on, on JVM in bytecode, we should do that."
  - 07:31: "if every other language does something else, that's uh, the clearest red flag to stop and pause and reconsider."

### What you were not told, that bears on the question today

1. `ZZ`'s own `narrow` and `widen`.
   - The 21:35 text named `ZZ` once, in the list of types that declare `narrow`. It did not say what `ZZ`'s `narrow` does. It did not name `ZZ`'s `widen`.
   - It said: "Widening always fits." That is false for `ZZ`'s `widen`. It goes from `ZZ` to `ZZ64` and can lose bits (row 502).
   - P-72 covers `ZZ64` to `ZZ32` and `NN64` to `NN32` only.
   - On 2026-09-28 the specification rung wrote that `ZZ`'s `narrow` keeps the low 32 bits too. It read P-72 as a general rule. You did not decide the `ZZ` case.
2. Who wrote them, and when.
   - Crink wrote `ZZ`'s `narrow` and `widen` on 2009-09-10 (`e1567d62f`). He reverted them the same day (`02e648434`) and put them back on 2009-09-11 (`8d2eb48f5`).
   - His commit message: "The nomenclature needs work, in my opinion. Incidentally, my first ever use of Java."
   - His comment on `widen`: "This routine, named for consistency, converts to a ZZ64".
   - `research/authorship.md:68` leaves Crink unresolved: "likely external SCA contributor".
   - You were told only who wrote the test: Steele.
3. The team's own signed `narrow` refused.
   - You were told: "The interpreter keeps the low bits: a plain cast." That was true for `NN64` only.
   - The team's walk `ZZ64` `narrow` called `Int.rc`. It stopped the run with "Overflow of ZZ32". This code is in the team's tree from 2008-03-24 (`1d2680d4d`) or earlier to its last commit, `a874948ac`.
   - Rung W's record said so (`rung-int-conversions/record.md:25`, row 347). The 21:35 text and rider 2 did not.
   - P-72's signed half removed that check on 2026-09-24 (`d6faad28f`).
4. Steele's checked `asZZ32` of 2011.
   - On 2011-09-08 Steele changed the compiled prelude's `asZZ32` from `jLongToInt` to `jLongOverflowingToInt` (`9ce7d8189`). The same commit made `+`, `-`, `·`, `DIV`, negation and absolute value on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` checked.
   - Rung W's `narrow` copied that body. Rung W gave four reasons for the throw (`rung-int-conversions/REPORT.md:74`). In the prelude, a plainly named operation checks. `asZZ32` checks. The team bound the unsigned helpers and used none. The specification has its general rule.
   - The 21:35 text gave the last reason only. It did not name `asZZ32`.
   - Today the compiled `trait ZZ64` has two conversions to `ZZ32` with two answers: `asZZ32` throws, `narrow` keeps the low bits (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:581`, `:659`; F-124).
5. The specification is silent on conversions, not only on `narrow`.
   - You were told that the word `narrow` is in no chapter. That is correct.
   - You were not told: no passage says what any written-out conversion does with a value that does not fit. The Working Draft's integer chapter has no fixed-size types.
   - One exception: the binary-words chapter declares `signedIndex()` and `unsignedIndex()` with `throws { IntegerOverflow }` (`Specification/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1292-1293`, `:1478-1479`). It describes neither, and the library does not build them.
6. The peers.
   - You were told the peers for the fixed-size types. That summary was fair.
   - You were not told the peers for an unbounded integer, the `ZZ` case. Java: `BigInteger.longValue()` keeps the low bits, `longValueExact()` throws. Scala: `BigInt.toLong` keeps the low bits. Swift: the plain conversion traps; the low bits are `truncatingIfNeeded:`. Julia: the plain conversion throws `InexactError`; the low bits are `x % Int64`. Rust: the `num-bigint` crate gives only checked conversions. (`explorations/reviews/widen-evidence.md`, section 7.)
   - Of the four peers that your principle names (P-66: Julia, X10, Swift, Rust), Swift and Julia check the plain conversion. Nobody checked X10.

### My judgements

These are mine, not the record's and not yours.

- The 21:35 text said: "Rung W's own unused import of the wrapping helper says the same." Rung W's report reads the same import block the other way: seven natives bound, one used for a conversion, and that one checks (`REPORT.md:52`). I see no evidence of intent in an unused import.
- The derivation called `narrow` on the unsigned types "a bit operation". That label was the coordinator's. P-66 says: "A hardware behaviour that bytecode can express gets its own explicit spelling". Read so, keeping the low bits is a hardware behaviour. That points to Swift's shape: a checked plain conversion, and a low-bits conversion with its own name. Your own words at 07:17 name Swift's trapping operators.
- Steele's test line 210 wrote `-x1` for 2^64-1. That needs a negation that wraps, and the line passed under walk until the revival changed it to `DOTMINUS x1` (`ab914b6e0`, 2026-09-26). The team's walk arithmetic on the fixed-size types wrapped (2026-09-23 07:42 text: "the interpreter's silently wrapping `+`, `-`, `·`"). So the 2008 test shows `narrow` in a world that wrapped. In 2011 Steele made the compiled prelude's arithmetic and `asZZ32` checked.
- At 06:49 on 2026-09-23 you were told: "No crossing on row 43". The queue line shows that you sent your approval at 21:48:12, before the coordinator's 21:48:38 "Row 43 still waits on your word". The gap that you felt was real. It does not change what you had read before you approved: the texts of 21:35:51 and 21:36:35.

### Why `narrow` came up then

- Rung W (climb batch 2, 2026-09-20) added `widen`, `narrow`, `unsigned` and `signed` to the compiler's prelude, on the four fixed-size types, because ladder files needed them (the 21:36:35 text). Its worker chose the throw and opened row 346. The re-approval table brought it to you as row 43.
- `ZZ`'s conversions were outside rung W. `ZZ`'s `widen` came up later as row 502. The specification rung (climb batch 6.5) stated `ZZ`'s `narrow` and left `widen` out, and its skeptic measured walk's `widen` (`widen-evidence.md`, section 4.1).
